transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-15 09:30 PST | Duration ~52m | Attendees: Priya Shah, Diego Alvarez, Maya Patel, Tom Reynolds, Svetlana Iakovleva

Summary:
Quick mid-pilot sync focused on improving KV/prefix cache hit rates and a pragmatic prefetch strategy to raise prompt reuse without hurting latency SLO. Discussed current numbers, where spend is coming from, and an action plan for a small canary.

Topics:
- Current KV/prefix hit baseline
- Prompt reuse heuristics and eviction policy
- Prefetch tradeoffs for cold sessions
- Measurement plan and canary rollout
- Security/PII notes for traces

00:00 Priya Shah: okay um hey everyone thanks for making time, uh this is the week two mid pilot, we're gonna run through the numbers Diego has, and then talk about prefetch prototypes and next steps
01:02 Diego Alvarez: (00:01) yeah hi all, I pulled the hit-rate charts and a couple of breakdowns, the baseline across the three test routes is ~22% kv hit overall, prefix-only hit around 14%, so end-to-end token savings about 6-7% when you factor in reuse plus batching, mm so not great yet
03:20 Maya Patel: can you repeat the 14% prefix figure? I thought our dashboard showed 18 last night, maybe different windows
03:33 Diego Alvarez: yeah there is a windowing diff, the rolling median for 7d is 17.8 but our pod sample for the last 24h shows 14.2, we think that's due to a spike in unique sessions from our mobile flow
04:50 Tom Reynolds: so mobile users are generating one-off prompts a lot, which hurts prefix reuse, correct?
05:06 Diego Alvarez: correct, and also many prompts have small personalization tokens at the end which break exact prefix matches
06:12 Priya Shah: right so that's where heuristic reuse comes in — we can do fuzzy-prefix matching or normalized templates, but that increases false-positive reuse and can change output. Diego can you show the false hit examples?
06:40 Diego Alvarez: sure uh (screen) here's a couple, user lines like "Plan route 5 for truck 42" vs "Plan route for truck forty-two" — those look similar but tokenized differently. We tried two normalization passes: numeric normalization + stopword stripping, that raised prefix bingo matches by ~9% but introduced a handful of hallucinated references in 0.3% of responses in the test set
09:05 Svetlana Iakovleva: small but concerning; we can't have hallucinations in PII contexts. Are those hallucinations when content is injected or when the model invents facts?
09:28 Diego Alvarez: more like content mis-assignment — the reused KV included a previously generated step that referenced a different city name, so output swapped in that city. Not ideal.
10:15 Priya Shah: yeah so safety-first rule: no reuse if any prompt contains PII tokens or location fields flagged by your sanitizer. Svetlana, can you confirm Aperture's PII tagging rules?
10:35 Svetlana Iakovleva: we already have a sanitizer that tags customer ids and address blocks; we'll share the rule set. For pilot we want tightening: if any tag present, do not reuse and do not prefetch.
11:12 Tom Reynolds: about prefetch — can you explain tradeoffs? We think prefetch could reduce latency for repeated journeys, but worried about cost and additional device/GPU load
12:02 Diego Alvarez: prefetch in our sense is running an ahead-of-time KV/encoder pass for likely next prompts. Two modes: soft-prefetch (cache keys only, no tokens decoded) and hard-prefetch (full partial decode up to N tokens). Soft-prefetch is lightweight and gives high hit-rate lift for templated flows; hard-prefetch increases GPU cycles and cost materially.
13:50 Priya Shah: Diego, what were your numbers for soft vs hard?
14:05 Diego Alvarez: in the test harness soft-prefetch bumped prefix hit to 28-30% on route A, with negligible tail latency increase. Hard-prefetch pushed to 36% but raised average GPU-ms per request by ~12% and the 95p latency for some sequences spiked by ~120ms under burst. So there's a cost/latency tradeoff.
16:40 Maya Patel: does that 95p spike occur only during busy periods?
16:52 Diego Alvarez: yeah mainly under concurrent burst > 200 qps on our shared dev pool; on dedicated it smooths out but still consumes more capacity so cost goes up.
17:30 Priya Shah: that's why we suggested a canary on a dedicated pool with 30% traffic — you get the hit-rate lift without impacting your primary latency SLO. If the spike happens, auto-fallback will route to a lower-cost baseline model.
18:00 Tom Reynolds: what about eviction — our current TTL is 10 minutes following the sample config, but we see some stale steps reused that are no longer relevant
18:23 Diego Alvarez: TTL tuning is critical. We recommend TTL per route based on observed average session length: for route A it's 4-6 minutes; for route B (planner) it's 20-30 minutes. We also support LRU-with-prefetch bias where newly prefetched keys get a probationary lower priority so they age faster unless reused.
20:05 Maya Patel: can Redwood's console surface per-key reuse and last-used timestamp? That would help our product team decide TTLs
20:20 Priya Shah: yes, Diego can wire a per-key table export — it has last_seen, hit_count, encoded_len, route_tag. We'll share a csv.
21:15 Diego Alvarez: note about measurement: depending on whether you count soft-prefetch as a 'hit' vs 'warm', the hit-rate jumps look different. We should align on definitions for the 2-week report.
22:02 Priya Shah: agreed. For the report we will include both: observed-kv-hit (actual cache hits during request), and prefetched-hit (key was prefetched and used).
23:10 Tom Reynolds: security — we're providing traces but must strip user ids. Svetlana will confirm the scrub.
23:30 Svetlana Iakovleva: yes we'll anonymize ids; we'll also mask any 9+ digit sequences and share via secure link.
24:05 Diego Alvarez: small note on tokenization mismatch — we have an encoder-agnostic normalizer that we'd like to run on your traces before we build prefix keys to avoid numeric/token differences. Prefer to do this on Redwood side or we can share a script you can run on your infra.
25:10 Maya Patel: prefer to run inside our environment first and share outputs with you; we'll need the script and a small readme.
26:00 Priya Shah: action: Diego to package normalizer and pipeline steps into a gist and workflow doc.
26:32 Diego Alvarez: sure. Also we saw some cache thrashing on route C due to high variability in prompt endings. We recommend a short suffix-trim step for that route to improve match.
27:55 Tom Reynolds: suffix-trim meaning drop trailing natural language tail? Does that change model output tone?
28:22 Diego Alvarez: there is risk — trimming can alter responses if the trailing tokens change intent. We propose a conservative trim: length-based trim of last 3 tokens only when similarity threshold is high. We'll AB test it.
30:10 Priya Shah: ok let's discuss the canary plan: two-week canary, start with soft-prefetch + normalized keys on dedicated pool at 30% traffic, monitor kv-hit, end-to-end latencies, and quality regression on a prompt set we both agree on
31:02 Diego Alvarez: quality monitoring: we'll run automated evals using your baseline prompt set and flag any regression >0.5 BLEU-ish proxy (we use embedding-similarity heuristics). Also manual spot checks for hallucination-prone flows.
33:20 Maya Patel: can we have a rollback threshold?
33:31 Priya Shah: yes — if model-output-quality drop exceeds our agreed threshold or 95p latency breaches 250ms above baseline for 5m windows, auto-roll back. We'll add that to the canary playbook.
35:05 Tom Reynolds: cost — show us delta between soft-prefetch, hard-prefetch and no-prefetch on monthly burn
35:20 Diego Alvarez: preliminary numbers: soft-prefetch adds ~6% to compute cost but saves about 9% on tokens billed; net delta ~ -3% (savings). Hard-prefetch roughly +10% compute and -12% token cost net ~ -2% savings but with higher peak load. We'll put exact spreadsheet in the follow-up.
37:10 Svetlana Iakovleva: regulatory note: need audit logs for prefetched keys, and KMS usage for any stored traces
37:30 Priya Shah: Redwood stores audit logs and integrates with customer KMS for private deployment; for Hosted we'll provide encrypted at rest and audit trails. We'll attach SOC2 sec bundle.
38:12 Maya Patel: excellent. A couple of minor transcript issues — sometimes Fireflies mislabels speakers, so apologies if names are off.
38:30 Priya Shah: no worries. Final recap: Diego shares normalized-key pipeline + CSV export, Maya/Svetlana share anonymized traces, Priya sends canary plan + pricing delta. Schedule: aim to kick canary the week of 2026-01-26.
40:05 Tom Reynolds: sounds good, thanks all.
